stories.headline: TREASURY BUYBACK RALLY FADES AS STOCKS SLIDE, 10-YEAR YIELD BACK TO 4.71%
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.87% to 7,641.16 and the Dow dropped 703.84 points (-1.32%) to 52,759.21 as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back to 4.71%, erasing most of Wednesday's relief rally sparked by the Treasury's debt-buyback announcement. Traders concluded the buyback plan addresses market liquidity, not the underlying supply of long-dated debt driving yields higher.
stories.explain: Buybacks let the Treasury retire older, less-liquid bonds using proceeds from new issuance, which narrows bid-ask spreads and briefly compresses the term premium — the extra yield investors demand for holding duration risk. But the government's overall borrowing need hasn't shrunk, so once the initial liquidity effect wears off, the same auction supply keeps pushing on yields from the other side. That's why a policy tool aimed at market plumbing produced only a one-day reprieve rather than a durable rate decline.

stories.headline: WALMART CRATERS 9.6% ON RARE SALES MISS, DRAGS DOW LOWER
stories.body: Walmart shares plunged to $103.35 despite beating on EPS ($0.81 vs. $0.74 est.) and revenue ($187.9B), as comparable sales grew just 2.6% against a 3.8% estimate — the retailer's first comp-sales miss in more than five years. Management cited shoppers pulling back under higher gas prices and guided Q3 EPS to $0.62-$0.64, below the $0.68 Street consensus.
stories.explain: Walmart's comparable-sales line is watched as a proxy for the price-sensitive consumer, since its customer base skews toward households most exposed to energy-cost swings. A miss there — even alongside a headline earnings beat — signals that this month's run-up in oil is already squeezing discretionary spending, exactly the kind of consumer-demand softening a supply-side oil shock can trigger without the Fed doing anything at all.

stories.headline: MARKETS BRACE FOR WARSH'S FIRST JACKSON HOLE SPEECH AS FED CHAIR
stories.body: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday, Aug. 28 — 19 days before the Sept. 16 FOMC decision — after minutes from the July meeting showed 'many participants' saw tightening as possibly necessary. Warsh has curtailed forward guidance at every opportunity since taking office in May, so any deviation from that pattern would carry outsized market impact.
stories.explain: Forward guidance is normally how a Fed chair manages market expectations between meetings, telegraphing intent so bond and equity markets can reprice gradually rather than react to a single decision. Warsh's deliberate refusal to do that removes the usual buffer, meaning traders have almost no signal to price off of until the speech itself lands — which raises the odds of a sharp, single-day repricing in yields regardless of what he actually says.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS FIFTH STRAIGHT GAIN, GOLD HOLDS NEAR $4,530 ON HORMUZ STANDOFF
stories.body: WTI crude rose to $86 (+2.1%) and Brent topped $93 as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed amid periodic Iranian attacks on shipping and retaliatory U.S. strikes, with no resolution in sight. Gold held near $4,533/oz, up modestly, as continued dollar weakness offset the drag from rising yields.
stories.explain: About a fifth of global oil supply transits the Strait of Hormuz, so a credible, ongoing closure prices in as a persistent risk premium rather than a one-time spike — which is why WTI has now risen for five straight sessions instead of reverting. Gold's resilience despite higher yields shows the safe-haven and dollar-weakness channels currently outweighing the usual drag from a higher opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.

stories.headline: DOLLAR SLIDES TO TWO-MONTH LOW EVEN AS TREASURY YIELDS CLIMB
stories.body: The dollar index (DXY) slipped to 98.76, its lowest level since late May, despite the 10-year yield's rise back to 4.71% — a divergence that would normally see the dollar strengthen. The index has now weakened roughly 2.4% over the past month.
stories.explain: Higher yields typically attract foreign capital into dollar assets, so a weaker dollar alongside rising rates suggests investors are pricing in something beyond the rate differential — in this case, skepticism that a Fed chair avoiding forward guidance and a hawkish-sounding minutes release will actually follow through with tightening. When the market doubts the credibility of hawkish signals, the usual yield-dollar relationship breaks down.

stories.headline: CALIFORNIA, OKLAHOMA COURTS GRANT ELIGIBILITY TROs, SCRAMBLING LATE-SUMMER PORTAL
stories.body: A California judge granted a temporary restraining order in the 5-in-5 eligibility lawsuit, giving players like Donovan Dent, Xaivian Lee, and Jaxon Kohler immediate eligibility and open access to the transfer portal; a similar TRO landed in Oklahoma covering players including Parsa Fallah. With over 70 new names now in the portal, rosters are still shifting weeks before the season — Oklahoma has already landed Villanova transfer Duke Brennan.

stories.headline: JAMES HARDEN AGREES TO RETURN TO CAVALIERS ON THREE-YEAR, $97M DEAL
stories.body: Harden is heading back to Cleveland on a three-year contract with a player option for 2028-29, part of a busy offseason stretch that also saw a multiteam trade send Peyton Watson to the Cavaliers and Max Strus to the Clippers. Russell Westbrook's Aug. 12 retirement announcement closed out an 18-year, nine-time All-Star career.

stories.headline: PRESEASON WEEK 2 HEADLINED BY HERBERT'S ONE-DRIVE CAMEO, RAIDERS-TEXANS
stories.body: Thursday's doubleheader features the Raiders at the Texans and the 49ers at the Chargers, where Justin Herbert is expected to run the first-team offense for exactly one drive. Elsewhere, Texans WR Jayden Higgins is out for the season with a torn ACL, and the Buccaneers ended DT Vita Vea's hold-in with a one-year extension.

stories.headline: ALABAMA'S QB BATTLE BETWEEN KEELON RUSSELL AND AUSTIN MACK GOES TO THE WIRE
stories.body: The Crimson Tide's starting job remains unsettled between five-star talent Keelon Russell and the steadier Austin Mack as fall camp winds down. Elsewhere, Virginia Tech had DT Kemari Copeland and TE Luke Reynolds named to the Senior Bowl Top 300, an early marker of this year's NFL draft-eligible talent.

deepDive.title: Why a Debt Buyback Couldn't Hold Down Long Yields
content: Wednesday's rally didn't last a full trading day. The Treasury's plan to more than double its buybacks of 10-, 20-, and 30-year debt pulled the 10-year yield down to roughly 4.65% and helped the S&P 500 post its first gain in four sessions. By Thursday, that yield was back to 4.71%, the S&P fell 0.87%, and the Dow shed more than 700 points. For a policy tool marketed as easing the pressure pushing long rates higher, a one-day effect is a strange result — and it says something specific about what buybacks can and can't actually do to the bond market.

Buybacks work on liquidity, not supply. The Treasury retires older, thinly-traded bonds by paying for them with proceeds from new issuance, which narrows bid-ask spreads and makes it easier for large investors to trade duration without moving the market. That reduces the term premium — the extra yield investors demand to hold long-dated debt through the uncertainty of future rate and inflation paths — because a more liquid bond is a less risky bond to hold. But the government's total borrowing need is unchanged. The same dollar amount of new debt still hits the market every auction cycle, so the underlying supply pressure never actually went away.

This is the same lesson from 2011's Operation Twist, when the Fed sold short-term Treasuries to buy long-dated ones and briefly flattened the curve — only for yields to re-normalize once the operation's balance-sheet effect stopped growing relative to net issuance. The durable drivers of long yields are the market's expected path of the Fed's policy rate, the net supply of Treasury debt investors must absorb, and where inflation expectations are anchored. Liquidity operations can smooth the path between those forces and today's price, but they can't override them. That's why Thursday's move looks less like a reversal and more like the market re-pricing back toward fundamentals once the initial liquidity boost faded.

That distinction matters heading into the next three weeks. Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole speech as Fed chair on Aug. 28, 19 days before the Sept. 16 FOMC decision, and he's been unusually disciplined about not pre-signaling policy. Walmart's rare comp-sales miss today is exactly the kind of soft-demand data point that argues against tightening, while July's minutes flagging possible tightening argue the opposite — a genuine split the Fed has to resolve. Watch the Treasury's actual auction sizes and inflation breakevens more than the buyback headline; those will decide whether 4.71% is a ceiling or a floor.
